title: Rabbi Chalafta (Abba Chalafta)
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-prepared translation; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.

paragraphs: The father of the well-known tanna Rabbi Yosi, and a descendant of Yonadav ben Rechav, as stated in the [Jerusalem Talmud, Taanit 4:2](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Taanit.4.2.13).[^1]

He is mentioned once in the Mishnah, in [Taanit 2:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Taanit.2.5): “It happened in the days of Rabbi Chalafta and Rabbi Hananiah ben Teradyon that someone went before the ark and completed the entire blessing, and they did not answer ‘Amen’ after him.”

He was already alive in the time of the Temple and saw Rabban Gamliel the Elder, as his son testifies in [Shabbat 115a](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.115a.7). Rabbi Yosi said: “It happened that Abba Chalafta”—Rashi explains that Rabbi Yosi’s father was named Chalafta—“went to Rabban Gamliel Beribbi in Tiberias and found him sitting at the table of R' Yohanan ben Nizuf. He said to him: ‘I remember your grandfather, Rabban Gamliel, standing on a step on the Temple Mount,’” and so forth. The account also appears near the beginning of [Tosefta Shabbat, chapter 14](https://www.sefaria.org/Tosefta_Shabbat.14.2), and in [Soferim 5:15](https://www.sefaria.org/Tractate_Soferim.5.15).[^2]

Now, since he had lived to see Rabban Gamliel the Elder, he must have been over thirty at the time of the destruction. Nevertheless, the Gemara in [Bava Kamma 70a–70b](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Kamma.70a.16-70b.3) is uncertain about the following account: Rabbi Yosi said, “When Abba Chalafta went to Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri to study Torah”—or, according to another version, Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri went to Abba Chalafta—“he said to him: ‘Suppose he enjoyed its produce …’”; the account continues, “But Rabbi Akiva disagrees about this.”[^3]

In [Tosefta Maaser Sheni 1:13](https://www.sefaria.org/Tosefta_Maaser_Sheni.1.13) and [Tosefta Bava Batra 2:4](https://www.sefaria.org/Tosefta_Bava_Batra.2.4), Rabbi Yosi says: “Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri came to [Abba] Chalafta … He said to him: ‘I too say so, but Akiva says …’” Likewise, in [Tosefta Oholot, chapter 5](https://www.sefaria.org/Tosefta_Oholot.5.7), Rabbi Yosi says: “Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri came to Abba Chalafta … ‘But Akiva declares it pure.’” From this we see that he was Rabbi Akiva’s colleague, since he called him simply “Akiva.” This is because his period of activity is reckoned with the generation of Rabbi Akiva and his associates, like that entire generation, whose members had also lived before the destruction.[^4]

He was the head in Sepphoris, as is stated in [Rosh Hashanah 27a](https://www.sefaria.org/Rosh_Hashanah.27a.13) and [Taanit 16b](https://www.sefaria.org/Taanit.16b.10): “This was Rabbi Chalafta’s practice in Sepphoris.” His colleague Rabbi Hananiah ben Teradyon was then the head in Sikhni, as stated there.[^5]

We have found no students attributed to him. Only his son Rabbi Yosi regularly mentions him as “Abba Chalafta,” as cited above. We also find in [Sotah 34a](https://www.sefaria.org/Sotah.34a.8): “Rabbi Yehuda said: Abba Chalafta, Rabbi Eliezer ben Matya, and Hananiah ben Hakhinai stood on those stones,” and so forth. (Possibly the meaning is that these three sages stood on the stones, but at different times, since Hananiah ben Hakhinai lived later than Rabbi Chalafta.)[^6]

In [Sanhedrin 80a](https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.80a.1-2), Rabbi Yosi says, “Even if Abba Chalafta is among them.” And in [Meilah 17b](https://www.sefaria.org/Meilah.17b.2), Rabbi Yosi says: “If Abba Chalafta were alive, could you say to him, ‘Give your son over to be killed’?”[^7]

It appears that he lived a long life. At the beginning of [Tosefta Kelim, Bava Batra, chapter 2](https://www.sefaria.org/Tosefta_Kelim_Batra.2.1), Rabbi Yosi says: “It happened that four elders were sitting privately with Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah in Sepphoris: Rabbi Hutzpit the interpreter, R' Yeshavav, and Rabbi [read: Abba] Chalafta.” This undoubtedly took place when the revolt of Betar began, or afterward.[^8]
His son Rabbi Yosi succeeded to his father’s position in Sepphoris, as explained in [his entry](https://www.girsology.com/toledot?entry=h-867aecd23abaf7b4).

He also had another son, who died without children. Rabbi Yosi, the deceased man’s brother, married his widow in levirate marriage, as stated at the beginning of [the Jerusalem Talmud, Yevamot](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Yevamot.1.1.6). R' Shimon ben Chalafta, however, was not his son, as explained in [that entry](https://www.girsology.com/toledot?entry=h-1e5e408c4fbf54df).[^9]

notes.text: The Yerushalmi calls Rabbi Yosi son of Chalafta a descendant of Yonadav ben Rechav; Hyman extends that ancestry to Chalafta. “Abba Chalafta” is Rabbi Yosi’s father, as Rashi explains on Shabbat 115a.

Hyman has “Yohanan ben Nizuf”; the Bavli reads Yohanan ha-Nazuf, “Yohanan the censured,” while the Tosefta has “Yohanan [ben Nozef].” Chalafta is the speaker recalling the elder Gamliel. “Beribbi” is a designation of distinction, not a patronymic.

The uncertainty concerns who visited whom. The abbreviated quotation concerns enjoying a field’s produce as evidence for a claim of possession. The story begins on Bava Kamma 70a and continues on 70b; Bava Batra 56b:3–4 is a parallel. The age “over thirty” is Hyman’s historical inference; the narrative gives no age or birth date.

The brackets around “[Abba]” reproduce Hyman’s proposed reading. Tosefta Bava Batra and Oholot have Rabbi Chalafta; Maaser Sheni has Chalafta without a title. Hyman compresses related reports on different legal subjects. He infers from the unadorned name “Akiva” that Chalafta was his colleague.
Hyman calls each sage הריש, “the head.” The passages describe communal practices without specifying a formal appointment to office.

Hyman abbreviates the reporting sage’s name אר״י; the Sotah passage names Rabbi Yehuda. “Those stones” are associated with the Israelites’ crossing of the Jordan. The suggestion that the three men visited them at different times is Hyman’s parenthetical explanation.
“Even if Abba Chalafta is among them” is a hypothetical legal example. The statement in Meilah is likewise counterfactual, referring to the danger of a mission under Roman persecution.

Hyman’s printed Tosefta subdivision is Kelim, Bava Batra, titled Tosefta Kelim Batra in the linked edition; Wikisource omits “Bava Batra.” חרש means “privately” here. Hyman abbreviates the list, which also includes Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri as the fourth elder. The bracketed replacement of “Rabbi” with “Abba,” and the dating to the Betar revolt, are Hyman’s judgments.

The Yerushalmi says that Rabbi Yosi ben Chalafta married his unnamed brother’s widow. Hyman refers to the separate biographies for Yosi’s succession in Sepphoris and his rejection of Shimon ben Chalafta as a son.
